title: Can a freeze dryer replace a freezer?
description: Electricity prices are sourced; a freezer's kilowatt-hours are not. What a freeze-drying cycle actually costs, and which foods it can and cannot replace.

faq.question: Can I unplug my freezer if I buy a freeze dryer?
faq.answer: Nothing in the published record supports that, and the published workflow points the other way. Preparation guidance for high-moisture foods is to pre-freeze for at least 24 hours before loading [26], Stay Fresh's manual specifies “a deep freezer for over 24 hours” [28], and Minnesota Extension notes that freezing food for 48 hours beforehand “may also speed up the freeze-drying process” [20]. A freeze dryer is documented as an appliance that assumes a freezer.

faq.question: Is freeze-dried food cheaper to store than frozen food?
faq.answer: We cannot say from these sources, and no page should pretend otherwise. The electricity price is published: 18.34 ¢/kWh residential for June 2026 [1]. A freeze-drying cycle has one checkable consumption figure at 18.5 kWh [5]. A home freezer's consumption appears in none of our sources, so the comparison has one side and not the other.

faq.question: What does one freeze-drying cycle actually cost in electricity?
faq.answer: At the only published figure that states both its rate and its duration, $3.33 for a 24-hour cycle at 18 ¢/kWh, or about 14 ¢ an hour [5]. At the current EIA residential average of 18.34 ¢/kWh [1], our own arithmetic on that same 18.5 kWh gives $3.39. Every other published claim in the category ($1.25 to $15 a batch across all sources) omits the rate, the duration, or both [6][10][18][15].

faq.question: How long does freeze-dried food really keep?
faq.answer: Two answers exist and they do not agree. Manufacturers publish up to 25 years in mylar with an oxygen absorber, stored cool, dark, dry and below 85°F, with fatty foods explicitly shorter [25][10]. Utah State states that “No real data exists on the shelf-life of home freeze-dried products” [15], UC ANR does not recommend consumption “beyond 5–10 years after processing” [21], and Iowa State states there is “no verification that food will last 25 years at this point” [22].

faq.question: Is freeze-dried food as safe as frozen food?
faq.answer: The process itself adds no safety step: “There is no heat treatment step in the freeze-drying process” [20], it “does not destroy harmful bacteria that can cause foodborne illness” [23], and bacteria “can survive the freeze-drying process and become active again when water is added back” [16]. That is why raw eggs and raw meat are where manufacturer guidance and extension guidance openly split [16][24].

howTo.name: Start from a kWh figure whose publisher stated its conditions
howTo.text: Use 18.5 kWh for a 24-hour cycle, the one figure in the category published alongside both its assumed rate and its assumed duration [5]. Do not start from a dollars-per-batch claim, because none of those state the inputs behind them [6][10][12].

howTo.name: Pick the right electricity rate and date it
howTo.text: Use the residential series, not the all-sector one: 18.34 ¢/kWh for June 2026 as a monthly figure [1], or 16.48 ¢/kWh for 2024 as an annual figure [2]. The 12.94 ¢/kWh all-sector figure on EIA's State Electricity Profiles page is not a household rate [4].

howTo.name: Multiply, and state the arithmetic rather than the result alone
howTo.text: 18.5 kWh at 18.34 ¢/kWh is $3.39 for a cycle [5][1]. Publishing the two inputs alongside the answer is what separates a checkable claim from the ones tabulated above.

bodyHtml:
The short version: for some foods and some households, yes. The honest reason it is not a cleaner answer is that half the arithmetic has never been published. The US residential electricity price averaged 18.34 cents per kilowatt-hour in June 2026, up 5.0% against June 2025 [1], and that price is the one input both appliances share. What a freeze-drying cycle consumes is published once in a checkable form, at 18.5 kWh for 24 hours [5]. What a home freezer consumes appears nowhere in the sources behind this page, so no freezer running cost is calculated here.

What a freezer costs to run

Here is the split before the numbers, because it decides how far this section can go: we have the price of electricity and not the freezer's consumption. The EIA publishes what a US household pays per kilowatt-hour, on two separate series that are easy to confuse with each other and with a third figure that is not residential at all. None of our sources publishes annual or per-day kilowatt-hours for a home freezer, so the second half of the multiplication is missing and is recorded again at the bottom of this page.

FigureWhat it actually isPeriodSource
18.34 ¢/kWhUS residential average, monthly (preliminary) series, up 5.0% year on yearJune 2026, released 2026-08-26[1]
16.48 ¢/kWhUS residential average, annual series (2023: 16.00)2024 data year[2]
42.86 ¢/kWhHighest state residential rate (Hawaii)2024 data year[3]
11.51 ¢/kWhLowest state residential rate (North Dakota)2024 data year[3]
12.94 ¢/kWhAll-sector average retail price — not residential2024 data year[4]

The last row is the one that quietly wrecks household arithmetic. The all-sector figure blends industrial and commercial sales into the average, which pulls it below what a house pays, and it is the headline number on EIA's own State Electricity Profiles page [4]. A monthly figure is also not an annual figure: 18.34 ¢/kWh describes a single month of a seasonal series [1], while 16.48 ¢/kWh describes the whole of 2024 [2]. Both are residential; neither substitutes for the other.

A note on the state figures: EIA publishes those tables in census-division order rather than rank order, so the highest and lowest above are produced by sorting EIA's own published values [3]. The values are the agency's; the ordering is ours.

What a freeze dryer costs to run

Every brand selling a home freeze dryer in the US under $5,000 publishes a dollars-per-batch figure, and exactly one publisher in the category states both the electricity rate and the cycle length behind its number. That makes it the only cost claim in the category a reader can reproduce, so it is the only one used for arithmetic here [5].

Stage of a 24-hour cycleEnergy, as publishedCost as published, at 18 ¢/kWh
Freezing, with a pre-chilled chamber0.5 kWh$0.09
Main drying, about 16 hours12 kWh$2.16
Final drying, about 7 hours6 kWh$1.08
Full cycle18.5 kWh$3.33, or about 14 ¢ an hour

All four rows are from one article [5], and three caveats travel with them. The figure is generic rather than tied to a model number. The rate it uses is the publisher's own statement that “the national average electricity rate is 18 cents per kwh,” dated May 2024 [5]. And the same article gives the freezing phase as “about 1-4 kWh” in its narrative while the $3.33 total rests on the smaller 0.5 kWh pre-chilled figure [5].

Our arithmetic, stated as ours: 18.5 kWh [5] at the EIA residential average for June 2026 of 18.34 ¢/kWh [1] is $3.39 for a 24-hour cycle. Nothing else on this page multiplies an unchecked figure by a rate.

What the rest of the category publishes is in the table below, and none of it is used in a calculation, because in every row either the rate or the duration or both are missing.

PublisherPublished claimWhy it cannot be checkedSource
Harvest Right, Small and Medium“approximately $1.25–$2.80 per batch depending on local electricity rates”No rate stated, no duration stated[6][7]
Harvest Right, Largeapproximately $2.00–$3.00 per batchNo rate stated, no duration stated[6][7]
Harvest Right, X-Largeapproximately $4.00 per batchNo rate stated, no duration stated[6][7]
Blue Alpine“about $2.00-$3.00 of electricity per day”; separately “a typical load will cost between $4 to $8”No rate stated, and the load figure is explicitly conditioned on “what kinds of bags are being used,” so it is not electricity alone[10]
Prep4Life“Most energy efficient freeze dryer in its class”No number, no definition of the class, no comparison published[12]
VEVORRated power 1550W in the spec table; 1500W in a Q&A on the same pageNo rate, no duration, and no cycle time published anywhere[13]
LanphanPower field reads “Confirm before quotation”The brand declines to publish power specifications at all[14]
University of Arizona Extension“approximately $1.50 (for a small load) to $3.50 (for a large load)” per cycleNo rate stated[18]
Utah State University Extension“between $2 to $5 worth of electricity per batch”; one East Coast consumer's bill “went up $20 to $30 a month during her heavy usage time”No rate stated for either figure[15]

One brand comes closer than the rest without arriving. Blue Alpine's Medium product page publishes “13 Amps Maximum Power Draw (1560W max)” and “9.0 Amps Average Power Draw (1080W average)” on the same page as “Average freeze-drying cycles take 12-20 hours”: power and duration together, which is most of what a reader needs [11]. What is missing is the rate, and the brand's separate dollar figures are published elsewhere without one [10].

Two independent metered owner reports exist, both on Harvest Right medium units, and both are secondary. One logged “an average electrical usage of 21 kW-hours/load” and about $1.90 a load, without ever stating the rate that produced the dollar figure [29]. The other measured with a Kill A Watt meter and concluded “20 kWh per run seems like a good estimate,” at $2.03 per run using $0.104/kWh, a rate quoted in 2022 and badly stale against 18.34 ¢ [30][1]. They converge on energy and diverge on cost for exactly the reason the whole category does.

The second report is also the only source anywhere that publishes both sides of the conversion: a typical load of “6 to 7 lbs (3 kg)” yielding “about 2 pounds (0.9 kg)” for 20 kWh [30]. Our arithmetic, again stated as ours: 20 kWh at 18.34 ¢/kWh [1] is $3.67 a run, or roughly $1.83 per finished pound, from one secondary report, one machine, one household. Treat it as the only per-pound figure that exists, not as a category number.

One published variable moves cost more than any of the disagreements above, and no brand prices it. The owner's manual states that a batch “that normally takes 24 hours to finish in a 75°F environment could take over 40 hours” in a hot room [9]. Nobody in the category publishes a cost figure conditioned on ambient temperature.

What you can and can't freeze-dry instead of freezing

The lead fact here is not about texture. “Freeze-drying does not kill bacteria. Instead, it preserves microorganisms in a dormant state,” says Jose Brandao of Utah State University Extension [17]. The University of Minnesota states the reason plainly: “There is no heat treatment step in the freeze-drying process” [20]. The University of Maine states the consequence: “Freeze drying does not destroy harmful bacteria that can cause foodborne illness” [23]. Utah State adds what happens on the other end: “Bacteria can survive the freeze-drying process and become active again when water is added back” [16]. That matters more here than it does for a freezer, because the finished product leaves the machine and is stored at room temperature [25].

What you would otherwise freezeWhat the sources establish about freeze-drying itSource
FruitSupported. Light-colored fruit such as apples, bananas and pears is pretreated with ascorbic acid or diluted lemon juice to prevent browning; fruit with skins is pierced or cut so moisture can escape[23][26]
VegetablesSupported with a pretreatment step: “Most vegetables need to be blanched” to prevent changes to color, texture and flavor[23][20]
Beans and other legumesSupported, conditioned: “Cooking or soaking improves texture after rehydration and helps prevent hard seed coats”[16]
Cooked meals, casseroles, pasta dishesSupported with a fat condition: “Casseroles or mixed foods will freeze dry well if they are not overly greasy.” Portions no thicker than about three-quarters of an inch, fat trimmed, grease blotted[19][24]
CheeseSupported, with a handling instruction for the fatty ones: “For high-fat cheeses, melt or blend and spread thinly before freeze-drying”[16]
Raw eggsContradicted. Manufacturers treat raw egg as routine; Utah State classifies it high-risk, states that Salmonella survives freeze-drying, and points to pasteurized liquid egg or fully cooked scrambled egg instead[16]
Raw meatContradicted. Harvest Right states meat “can be freeze dried raw or cooked”; Utah State requires it be “fully cooked either before freeze-drying or after rehydration”[24][16]
Bread and baked goodsContradicted. Harvest Right publishes a preparation guide; Iowa State states “High-fat foods, high-sugar foods, and baked goods (breads, cakes, muffins) do not freeze dry successfully”[24][22]
Butter, peanut butter, mayonnaise, chocolateAdvised against. “Freeze drying removes water, but oil remains.” Utah State names mayonnaise specifically: high-fat foods “do not freeze-dry well and can become unsafe.” Blue Alpine lists peanut butter and honey as exceptions to its own machine[24][17][10]
HerbsSupported, and they skip the rehydration step entirely: “There is no need to rehydrate herbs, onions, or bell peppers as they can be added directly to foods”[22]

Then there is the claim the whole substitution rests on. Harvest Right states that “Many properly packaged freeze-dried foods can last up to 25 years or longer under ideal conditions,” attached to a mylar bag with an oxygen absorber, stored cool, dark, dry and below 85°F, and conditioned on fat: “Foods that contain higher amounts of fat generally have shorter storage lives” [25]. Blue Alpine publishes “25+ years” on the same packaging condition [10]. Three extension services push back, and none of them softens it. Utah State: “No real data exists on the shelf-life of home freeze-dried products,” anchoring instead to an 8-to-10-year conservative estimate for commercially produced product in metal-mylar pouches [15]. UC ANR: the claim “has not been corroborated by university studies for home freeze dryers,” and “Consuming home-frozen-dried products is not recommended beyond 5–10 years after processing” [21]. Iowa State: “There is no verification that food will last 25 years at this point” [22]. No storage figure on this page is a promise; each one is a reading of what its publisher published.

The packaging condition is not decorative. Sealing the wrong thing does not help: the outside of a piece “can feel completely dry even when moisture remains in the center,” which is why Harvest Right's own instruction is to break open the largest pieces from several trays and check the middle before packaging [27].

The honest comparison

Set out side by side, the comparison people actually ask for cannot be completed from published sources, and the blank column is the finding rather than an omission.

QuestionHome freezerHome freeze dryer
Price of the electricity it uses18.34 ¢/kWh, US residential, June 2026 [1]The same rate [1]
Energy per unit of workNot in our sources18.5 kWh per 24-hour cycle, checkable [5]; 20–21 kWh metered, secondary [29][30]
Purchase priceNot in our sources$1,595 to $4,995 across the brands selling under $5,000 [8][14]
Electrical installationNot in our sourcesA dedicated 15-amp circuit for the smaller sizes and a dedicated 20-amp circuit for the largest; “Do not use an extension cord” [7][9]
Time to process one batchNot in our sources“between 13 hours and 35 hours” for most foods; a 24-hour batch “could take over 40 hours” in a hot room [7][9]
Where the output is storedNot in our sourcesRoom temperature, cool, dark, dry, below 85°F, in mylar with an oxygen absorber [25]
How long the output keepsNot in our sourcesManufacturers: 25 years [25][10]. Extension services: 5–10 years, and no verification of the longer figure exists [21][22][15]
Does it include a pathogen kill step?Not in our sourcesNo. “There is no heat treatment step” [20]; the process does not kill bacteria [17][23]
Does it need the other appliance?Not in our sourcesYes, in the published workflow. Pre-freezing in a household or deep freezer for 24 to 48 hours is instructed by the manufacturers and by extension [26][28][20]

That last row is the one that answers the title most directly. The published preparation guidance for high-moisture foods (milk, eggs, soups, stews) is to pre-freeze for at least 24 hours before loading [26], with Stay Fresh's manual specifying “a deep freezer for over 24 hours” [28] and Minnesota noting that freezing prepared food “for 48 hours before filling the trays may also speed up the freeze-drying process” [20]. On the documentation as it stands, a freeze dryer is an appliance that assumes a freezer, not one that retires it.

Who this works for

These are conditions, not a recommendation, and each one is somebody's published requirement rather than our opinion.

  • There is a dedicated circuit where the machine will sit. Small, medium and large models are specified on a dedicated 15-amp circuit and the X-Large on a dedicated 20-amp circuit, with extension cords ruled out and, in the owner's manual only, GFI outlets and surge protectors ruled out too [7][9].
  • The room stays inside the published band. The manual states “This device is designed for indoor installation only” and, in the same document, a recommended range of 35–90°F, a hard limit of “not above 95°F…or below 35°F,” and a warranty-voiding ceiling of 105°F [9]. Heat is also the cost variable nobody prices [9].
  • The noise lands somewhere you can live with. The one independent measurement in the category puts it at “62 to 67 decibels” when the vacuum pump turns on, against a vacuum cleaner at 70 dB, published in 2019, with no measurement distance stated [15].
  • Your batch expectations survive contact with the disagreement. Harvest Right publishes 6–10 lb of fresh food per batch for the Small, 10–15 for the Medium, 18–27 for the Large and 40–50 for the X-Large [8]; Utah State Extension published 4–7, 7–10 and 12–16 lb for the first three sizes [15]. Both stand as published.
  • The food you want to preserve is on the supported side of the table above. If it is raw egg, raw meat or bread, you are choosing between a manufacturer and an extension service, not following a settled answer [16][22][24].
  • You are keeping the freezer. The published workflow pre-freezes in one [26][28][20].
  • You hold a 5-to-10-year expectation rather than a 25-year one, which is what the extension services recommend and what the absence of verification supports [21][15][22].

What we could not source

  • A home freezer's energy consumption. Nothing in our sources publishes kilowatt-hours per year, per day or per cubic foot for a home freezer, so the freezer column above carries a rate [1][2] and no consumption, and no freezer running cost is computed anywhere on this page. This is the single largest gap in the comparison.
  • A checkable manufacturer cost claim. Not one brand selling a home freeze dryer in the US under $5,000 publishes a cost claim that states both its assumed rate and its assumed cycle duration [6][10][12][13][14]. The only checkable figure in the category is a generic blog calculation resting on a May-2024 rate [5].
  • Any energy label or test procedure for this appliance class. No EnergyGuide label, no DOE test procedure and no ENERGY STAR specification was found for home freeze dryers, which means no manufacturer's figure is comparable to another's by any defined method.
  • Metered data for any brand other than Harvest Right. Both independent measurements are on Harvest Right medium units and both are secondary [29][30]. Nothing metered exists for the other brands.
  • Cost per pound of finished food, from any primary source. One secondary report publishes both the input weight and the output weight [30]; every other cost figure in the category is per batch, and batches range from 6–10 lb to 40–50 lb [8], which makes per-batch figures non-comparable across machine sizes.
  • Monthly state-level residential rates. EIA publishes them only inside a spreadsheet (Table 5.6.A), which could not be read in this environment. The state figures above come from the annual table instead, and are labeled as annual [3].
  • A cost figure conditioned on ambient temperature, even though the manual says heat can nearly double a cycle [9].
  • Verification of the 25-year storage claim. Three extension services state that it does not exist [15][21][22].
  • Any ranking. No source orders these machines, or these two appliances, on running cost, loudness, or maintenance burden, and the published figures are not comparable enough to support one. None is offered here.
  • Sublime Pantry has bench-tested no freeze dryer, no freezer and no food. Every figure above is a reading of somebody else's published page on a stated date.
